format.melody: Bars separated by |. A note is letter + optional # or b (## / bb) + octave + duration (w h q e s = whole, half, quarter, eighth, sixteenth), then optional . If the tune has a pickup, the first bar holds only the pickup beats.
format.chords: One entry per full bar (no chord for the pickup), separated by |. Several chords in a bar split it evenly, or give beats with Chord:beats. Qualities: (major) m 7 m7 maj7 dim dim7 m7b5 6 m6 aug sus4 9.

format.liner: Liner notes shown under the sheet: origins (where the song comes from), tradition (how it is traditionally played), listen (recordings worth hearing), try (a way to practise that style here). Keep facts sourced and hedge anything uncertain.

tunes.composer: French folk melody (“Ah! vous dirai-je, maman”)
tunes.year: Melody printed 1761 · words by Jane Taylor, 1806

liner.origins: The tune is French. It was printed in Paris in 1761 and sung as “Ah! vous dirai-je, maman,” a child complaining to her mother. In 1806 the English poet Jane Taylor published “The Star,” the poem we now sing as “Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star,” in a book of nursery rhymes she wrote with her sister Ann. The same melody carries “Baa, Baa, Black Sheep” and the Alphabet Song, which a Boston publisher copyrighted in 1835. Around 1781 Mozart, then in his twenties in Vienna, wrote twelve piano variations on it (K. 265).
liner.tradition: Because it moves by step and repeats its phrases, it is many musicians’ first tune. The Suzuki violin method opens with “Twinkle Variations,” where students play the same melody in a series of different rhythms before they learn anything else. Mozart’s variations show the opposite end: the tune stays in the background while runs, minor-key turns and ornaments decorate it. Teachers use it to practise call and response, rhythm games and transposition.
listen: Mozart, Twelve Variations on “Ah vous dirai-je, Maman,” K. 265 (any piano recording)
Suzuki Violin School, Book 1: “Twinkle Variations”
liner.try: Play it with each Rhythm setting in turn, the way Suzuki students do. Then pick Upside down and ask whether it is still the same tune.

liner.origins: A French round about Brother John, a friar who has overslept and missed ringing the morning bells (“sonnez les matines”). The oldest known copy is a Paris manuscript from about 1780. Some researchers have linked it to the composer Jean-Philippe Rameau, but nobody knows for certain who wrote it. It travelled with the words translated: “Are You Sleeping, Brother John?” in English, “Bruder Jakob” in German, and “Two Tigers” in Chinese.
liner.tradition: It is built to be sung as a round: up to four groups enter two bars apart and the parts fit together because every phrase outlines the same chord. In 1888 Gustav Mahler turned it into a slow minor-key funeral march in the third movement of his First Symphony, opening with a solo double bass. Playground versions speed up each time through; choirs use it to teach singing in parts.
listen: Mahler, Symphony No. 1, third movement (the minor-key round on solo double bass)
liner.try: Split the room into groups and sing it as a round over the band. Then try Upside down: the inverted tune still works as a round.

tunes.about: Beethoven’s tune moves almost entirely by step, one scale note at a time. Try “Chord tones” and “Skeleton” to hear the harmony underneath it.
tunes.source: Beethoven, Symphony No. 9, Op. 125 (1824), in its original key of D; public domain. Chords simplified for this page.

liner.origins: Beethoven set Friedrich Schiller’s poem “An die Freude” (1785) in the finale of his Ninth Symphony, first performed in Vienna on 7 May 1824. He had sketched settings of the poem for decades. By the premiere he was almost completely deaf; the story goes that a singer had to turn him round to see the audience applauding. It was the first symphony by a major composer to bring singers and a chorus into the final movement.
liner.tradition: The orchestra introduces the tune quietly in the cellos and basses, then passes it up through the orchestra before the voices take it. Listen for the famous jolt in the second half: one note arrives a beat early, tied across the bar line. The melody became the hymn “Joyful, Joyful, We Adore Thee” (1907) and, without words, the anthem of Europe. Leonard Bernstein conducted the symphony in Berlin at Christmas 1989, after the Wall came down, and changed the word “Freude” (joy) to “Freiheit” (freedom).
listen: Beethoven, Symphony No. 9, fourth movement (the theme first appears in the low strings)
Leonard Bernstein, Berlin, December 1989 (“Ode to Freedom”)
liner.try: Play it slowly in Melody + click, then switch to Chord tones and Skeleton to hear how little the harmony moves under a tune that moves by step.

liner.origins: An African American spiritual about the hope of joining the saints in heaven. It was sung in Black churches in the South long before anyone wrote it down, and similar gospel hymns were printed in the 1890s. Louis Armstrong’s 1938 recording turned it into a jazz hit, and it became the tune most associated with New Orleans.
liner.tradition: In a New Orleans jazz funeral the brass band plays hymns slowly as a dirge on the way to the cemetery, then breaks into a fast, joyful “Saints” on the way back while the “second line” of neighbours dances behind. Bands play it in a two-beat feel and pass the melody between trumpet, clarinet and trombone, which play different lines at once (collective improvisation). Crowds sing along and answer the leader’s lines.

Any New Orleans brass band, such as the Preservation Hall Jazz Band or the Dirty Dozen Brass Band
liner.try: Play it once as a dirge (Ballad band, slow tempo), then go to Two-beat at a quick tempo, the way a funeral band turns for home.

liner.origins: John Newton, an English sailor who had worked in the Atlantic slave trade and later became a clergyman and opponent of it, wrote the words for a New Year’s Day sermon in 1773. They were published in Olney Hymns in 1779. The tune, called “New Britain,” is an American folk melody from the shape-note singing books of the early 1800s. William Walker joined Newton’s words to it in his book Southern Harmony (1835), and that pairing stuck.
liner.tradition: It is sung many ways: in four-part shape-note harmony, in the slow “lined-out” style of African American churches where a leader calls each line and the congregation answers with long, ornamented notes, and with gospel melisma (many notes on one syllable) as Mahalia Jackson and Aretha Franklin sang it. Its five-note scale fits the bagpipes, and a pipe band version topped the British charts in 1972. Singers stretch the tempo freely.

liner.origins: Julia Ward Howe wrote new words for a tune already sung as “John Brown’s Body.” Her poem appeared in The Atlantic Monthly in February 1862, during the American Civil War. William Steffe is commonly credited with the older camp-meeting melody, though the tune’s early history is not fully settled.
liner.tradition: The song joins three long verse lines to the repeated “Glory, glory, hallelujah” refrain, sung to the same tune as “John Brown’s Body.” Singers often broaden the last line, “His truth is marching on.”

tunes.about: A minor key. The G♯ is borrowed from the harmonic minor scale to lead back to A. The same tune became the carol “What Child Is This?” (1865).

liner.origins: A ballad called “A New Northern Dittye of the Lady Greene Sleeves” was registered in London in 1580. A popular legend says Henry VIII wrote it for Anne Boleyn, but the tune is built on Italian chord patterns (the romanesca and passamezzo antico) that reached England after Henry died. Shakespeare mentions it twice in The Merry Wives of Windsor, so audiences of the 1590s already knew it.
liner.tradition: In the Renaissance it was played on lute and viols, with players adding new variations over the repeating chords each time round. In 1865 William Chatterton Dix wrote the Christmas words “What Child Is This?” to it. Ralph Vaughan Williams used it in his opera Sir John in Love, and his Fantasia on Greensleeves (1934) made it an orchestral favourite. John Coltrane recorded it in 1961 as a modal jazz waltz. Players choose between the raised and plain sixth and seventh notes of the minor scale, which changes its colour.

liner.origins: “Auld lang syne” is Scots for “old long since”: days gone by. In 1788 Robert Burns sent the poem to a collection of Scottish songs, saying he had taken it down from an old man’s singing, though he probably added verses himself. It was first printed with a different melody; the tune everyone sings now was paired with the words in George Thomson’s Select Scottish Airs in 1799.
liner.tradition: It is sung at Hogmanay, the Scottish New Year, and then around the world at midnight on 31 December. Singers stand in a circle holding hands, and on the last verse cross their arms and join hands with the people on either side. In the United States, Guy Lombardo’s band played it on New Year’s radio and TV broadcasts from 1929 for nearly fifty years. In Japan the same tune, as “Hotaru no Hikari,” is sung at graduations and played when shops close.
listen: Any Hogmanay recording with pipes and voices

liner.try: Try the Short–long rhythm to hear the Scotch snap, a short note on the beat followed by a long one, which is a fingerprint of Scottish fiddle music.

tunes.about: A 6/8 double jig in AABB form: two groups of three eighth notes per bar. Each eight-bar strain is played twice; feel two large pulses rather than six equal beats.
tunes.source: Traditional melody, public domain. This G-major setting follows the session transcription at https://thecelticroom.org/abc-tune-library.html (The Irish Washerwoman, X:17), with final notes regularized for the AABB practice form. Compare the 1837 Blackshaw manuscript setting at https://www.village-music-project.org.uk/?page_id=348 . Chords and jig backing arranged for this page.

liner.origins: The tune circulated around Britain, Ireland and North America under several titles. A nineteenth-century manuscript already records “The Irish Washerwoman”; exact origins are debated. Tune history and variants: https://ibiblio.org/fiddlers/IP_IZ.htm
liner.tradition: A double jig has six eighth notes per bar, grouped three plus three. Sessions commonly repeat the eight-bar A and B strains (AABB) before moving to another tune.
listen: Listen to a traditional fiddle or whistle performance and tap only the two main pulses in each bar.
liner.try: Loop bars 1–8 until the two-pulse feel settles, then practise bars 17–24. Turn off the melody and play AABB with the jig band.

tunes.about: The 12-bar blues: four bars on I, two on IV, two on I, then V, IV, I, V. The riff moves to fit each chord. Use Trade fours to improvise your own riff in the empty bars.
tunes.source: Written for this site; free for any classroom to copy, play and change.

liner.origins: This riff was written for ClassroomOS, but the form is about 120 years old. The blues grew in African American communities in the Deep South in the late 1800s out of work songs, field hollers and spirituals. By the 1910s songwriters such as W. C. Handy were publishing blues in the 12-bar form you see here: three four-bar lines over the I, IV and V chords.
liner.tradition: Blues lyrics often follow an AAB pattern: a line, the same line again, then an answer. Instruments do the same with riffs, short phrases repeated and moved to fit each chord, a sound Kansas City bands like Count Basie’s built whole arrangements on. Players bend into the “blue” notes between major and minor, answer each other in call and response, and take turns soloing chorus after chorus.
listen: Count Basie Orchestra, “One O’Clock Jump” (1937), a riff-built blues
Bessie Smith with Louis Armstrong, “St. Louis Blues” (1925)
liner.try: Use Trade fours: answer the riff with your own four bars. Write a three-line AAB lyric about your day and sing it over the band.

tunes.about: Handy wrote it in 1914 with three distinct strains; this is the famous 12-bar chorus in G. The flattened “blue notes” on B♭ give it its unmistakable character.
tunes.source: Melody transcribed from the original 1914 Pace & Handy Music Co. sheet music (chorus strain, 2/4 notated in 4/4); public domain. Chords added for this page.

liner.origins: W. C. Handy, later called “the Father of the Blues,” published it in Memphis in 1914 through his own company, Pace & Handy. He said it was inspired by a woman he heard in St. Louis singing about the man who had left her. Handy built it from three strains, including a minor section in a tango (habanera) rhythm, mixing blues with the Latin dance rhythms popular at the time.
liner.tradition: It became one of the most recorded songs of the first half of the twentieth century. Bessie Smith’s 1925 version with Louis Armstrong’s cornet answering her lines is the model for blues singing with an instrument: call and response. Bands play the 12-bar strain in a loose two-beat swing, lean on the blue notes, and often slip into the tango rhythm for the minor section, which is not included in this lead sheet.
listen: Bessie Smith with Louis Armstrong (1925)
Bessie Smith in the short film St. Louis Blues (1929), her only film
liner.try: Play Band only and answer each two-bar vocal phrase with a two-bar fill, as Armstrong did for Bessie Smith.

tunes.about: A 16-bar chorus that became one of the foundational jam-session tunes in early jazz (and the harmonic source for Miles Davis’s “Donna Lee”). Starts with a short pickup before bar 1.
tunes.source: Melody transcribed from the original 1917 Shapiro, Bernstein & Co. sheet music; public domain. Chords added for this page.

liner.origins: James F. Hanley wrote the music and Ballard MacDonald the words in 1917, a sentimental song about going home to Indiana. The Original Dixieland Jass Band recorded it the same year, among the very first jazz records, and it became a jam-session standard. Since 1946 it has been sung before the start of the Indianapolis 500 motor race; Jim Nabors sang it there most years from 1972 to 2014.
liner.tradition: Dixieland and swing bands play it fast, often opening a set with it: Louis Armstrong’s All Stars used it as their theme. Bebop musicians kept the chords and wrote new melodies over them, a practice called a contrafact. “Donna Lee” (1947), recorded by Charlie Parker, is the famous example; Miles Davis said he wrote it. Players treat the chords as a racetrack for improvising long lines of eighth notes.
listen: Original Dixieland Jass Band (1917)
Louis Armstrong and His All Stars
Charlie Parker, “Donna Lee” (1947), new melody over the same chords
liner.try: Turn the melody off (Band only) and make up a new tune over the chords. That is how “Donna Lee” was born.

tunes.about: A 20-bar chorus instead of the usual 32: it starts away from home on the IV chord (E♭) and borrows its minor (E♭m6) on the way back to B♭, a move players still call the “After You’ve Gone” sound. A Dixieland and swing jam favorite, recorded by Bessie Smith, Louis Armstrong and Benny Goodman.
tunes.source: Melody from the concert lead sheet by the New Orleans Jazz Museum’s Public Domain Project (prepared by Evan Christopher), based on the original 1918 published sheet music; public domain. Common-practice chords. Chorus only; the verse is not included.

liner.origins: Turner Layton (music) and Henry Creamer (words) were an African American songwriting team in New York. Their song was a hit for the singer Marion Harris in 1918. Layton later moved to London and became a star in the piano-and-voice duo Layton & Johnstone. The lyric warns a lover that they will regret leaving.
liner.tradition: Singers often begin with the verse, sung freely out of tempo, then the band kicks into the chorus. Bessie Smith (1927) sang it as a blues; Louis Armstrong (1929) and the Benny Goodman Trio (1935) turned it into a fast showcase, with drum breaks and chorus after chorus of improvising. Judy Garland sang it in the film For Me and My Gal (1942). In Dixieland jams it is a tempo test: how fast can the band go and still swing?

Bessie Smith (1927)
Louis Armstrong (1929)
Benny Goodman Trio (1935)
liner.try: Start at 120 BPM, then raise the tempo by 8 BPM each chorus. Listen for the E♭ to E♭m6 move, the heart of the tune.

tunes.about: A classic 32-bar AABA standard recorded by Miles Davis, John Coltrane, and countless others. The repeated quarter-note motifs make it ideal for practicing phrasing.
tunes.source: Melody transcribed from the original 1926 Jerome H. Remick & Co. sheet music; public domain. Chords adapted for this page.

liner.origins: Ray Henderson (music) and Mort Dixon (words) wrote it in 1926, a cheerful song about leaving troubles behind and heading home. Gene Austin’s recording that year was a big hit, and it stayed in the repertoire of dance bands and singers through the 1930s.
liner.tradition: Jazz musicians remade it in the 1950s. Miles Davis played it at a relaxed medium tempo on ’Round About Midnight (1957), using a Harmon mute and leaving lots of space between phrases; John Coltrane followed with long, dense lines. That contrast, few notes against many, is still how players learn it. Singers often slow it down and change the rhythm of each phrase.

Miles Davis, ’Round About Midnight (1957)
John Coltrane, Bye Bye Blackbird (live in Stockholm, 1962)
liner.try: Play the melody with long rests between phrases, as Miles did. Then try Push the beat and hear how much swing a few anticipations add.

tunes.about: Originally from the 1928 operetta The New Moon, this became an up-tempo jazz vehicle for Charlie Parker, Billie Holiday, and Dizzy Gillespie.
tunes.source: Melody transcribed from the original 1928 Harms Inc. sheet music; public domain. Chords added for this page.

liner.origins: Sigmund Romberg (music) and Oscar Hammerstein II (words) wrote it for The New Moon (1928), an operetta set in eighteenth-century New Orleans. In the show it is a soaring romantic ballad. Its bridge closely follows a melody from Tchaikovsky’s piano piece “June” (Barcarolle) from The Seasons.
liner.tradition: Jazz musicians sped it up. Billie Holiday recorded it in 1944, and bebop players turned it into a fast vehicle for improvising. The A sections sit on long chords that leave room for running lines, while the minor bridge changes the mood. Many bands play the head at a racing tempo and drop the ballad feel completely.

Tchaikovsky, The Seasons: “June” (to hear where the bridge comes from)
liner.try: Play it once with the Ballad band at a slow tempo, then with Swing at 200 BPM or faster. Same tune, two worlds.

liner.origins: Another song from Romberg and Hammerstein’s The New Moon (1928). Despite the gentle title, in the show it is a cynical song about love: it starts as softly as a sunrise and can end in betrayal. It was written with a tango rhythm.
liner.tradition: Artie Shaw’s band swung it in 1938, but modern jazz made it a classic. The Modern Jazz Quartet, Sonny Rollins (A Night at the Village Vanguard, 1957) and John Coltrane (Live at the Village Vanguard, 1962) all recorded it. Bands often play a Latin or vamp feel on the minor A sections and swing the bridge, and use the minor ii–V chords as a playground for long solos.

tunes.about: Waller wrote this milestone 32-bar ballad for Connie’s Hot Chocolates in Harlem in 1929. The syncopated eighth-note figures swing naturally against the walking changes.
tunes.source: Melody transcribed from the original 1929 Mills Music Inc. sheet music; public domain. Chords added for this page.

liner.origins: Fats Waller and Harry Brooks wrote the music and Andy Razaf the words for Connie’s Hot Chocolates (1929), a revue that started at Connie’s Inn in Harlem and moved to Broadway. A young Louis Armstrong played it from the orchestra pit during the show, and his 1929 recording made him a star with a wide audience. Waller recorded his own piano version the same year.
liner.tradition: Waller was a master of Harlem stride piano: the left hand leaps between a low bass note on beats 1 and 3 and a chord on beats 2 and 4, while the right hand plays the tune and fills. Singers deliver it with a wink, playing with the rhythm of the words. In 1978 a Broadway revue of Waller’s songs, Ain’t Misbehavin’, won the Tony Award for Best Musical.

liner.try: On piano, play the bass note on beats 1 and 3 and the chord on 2 and 4: that is the stride left hand. Use the Chords tab to find each shape.

tunes.about: Cole Porter’s masterpiece blends major and minor tonalities over a 32-bar form. Jazz musicians frequently play it at blistering tempos (and Tadd Dameron based “Hot House” on its chords). Features quarter-note triplets in the bridge.
tunes.source: Melody transcribed from the original 1929 Harms Inc. sheet music; public domain. Chords adapted for this page.

liner.origins: Cole Porter wrote it for the revue Wake Up and Dream, which opened in London and then on Broadway in 1929. Porter said the melody grew from music he heard in Marrakesh, Morocco. Each A section starts in a minor colour and resolves to major, which gives the tune its question-and-answer feeling.
liner.tradition: Jazz musicians love its chords: every A section is a chain of ii–V moves. In 1945 Tadd Dameron wrote a new bebop melody over them, “Hot House,” recorded by Dizzy Gillespie and Charlie Parker. Clifford Brown and Max Roach played it at a blistering tempo. Bands often add a Latin feel to the A sections or start with a vamp.

liner.origins: Fats Waller (music) and Andy Razaf (words) wrote it in 1929 for Load of Coal, a floor show at Connie’s Inn in Harlem. Waller’s own 1934 recording with his small band, Fats Waller and His Rhythm, made it a hit, full of his jokes and asides.
liner.tradition: Its riff-like A section, the same small phrase repeated over the two-chord ii–V, made it perfect for jam sessions and big bands. Count Basie’s band played it, and in Paris in 1937 Django Reinhardt recorded it with Coleman Hawkins and Benny Carter. Charlie Parker wrote “Scrapple from the Apple” over its A section chords. Musicians often answer the riff back and forth between sections of the band.

tunes.about: Introduced by Ethel Merman in Girl Crazy, this song’s chord progression (“rhythm changes”) became the most played harmonic sequence in jazz after the 12-bar blues. Includes the original 2-bar tag ending (34 bars total).

liner.origins: George Gershwin (music) and Ira Gershwin (words) wrote it for the musical Girl Crazy (1930). Ethel Merman, in her Broadway debut, held a high note for sixteen bars and stopped the show. The pit band that night included future jazz stars Benny Goodman, Glenn Miller and Gene Krupa. Gershwin later wrote Variations on “I Got Rhythm” (1934) for piano and orchestra.
liner.tradition: Its chords, called “rhythm changes,” became the most played progression in jazz after the 12-bar blues. Musicians wrote hundreds of new tunes over them: “Anthropology,” “Oleo,” “Cotton Tail,” even the theme from The Flintstones. Players race through the A sections and then take the bridge’s chain of dominant chords (III7–VI7–II7–V7) as a challenge. Many players drop the two-bar tag that ends this original version.

tunes.about: A slow minor blues about grief at a hospital morgue (“I went down to St. James Infirmary, saw my baby there”). Each verse is eight bars: the tune opens on a rising A–C–E minor arpeggio, and the harmony is just Am and E7 plus one chromatic color chord, F7, that slides down to E7 (F7 → E7 → Am). This chart plays the pattern twice, one chorus per verse. Jazz players usually take it in C minor; this lead sheet sits in A minor so it lies under the fingers on most instruments.
tunes.source: Traditional melody, notated here as a simplified practice arrangement from the widely sung folk tune (the song is a folk-blues with no single authoritative score). Chords simplified for this site; compare it with recordings and note where singers bend the melody.

liner.origins: The song grew out of an old British street ballad, “The Unfortunate Rake” (also “The Unfortunate Lad”), in which a dying soldier or young man is mourned by those he loved. In the United States the story moved to a hospital and a morgue, and the tune turned into a blues. Its authorship is unknown; Irving Mills published an arrangement in 1929–30 under the name Joe Primrose, but the song is much older than that credit.
liner.tradition: Sung and played slow, almost like a funeral march, with a steady four-beat pulse and plenty of space between the lines. A common arrangement starts with a vocal intro of Am – E7 – Am played twice, then sings verse after verse over the same eight bars, changing the words each time. Singers tell the story and bend the melody freely, so no two performances match.

Listen for the F7 chord: it sits a half step above E7, and the slide F7 → E7 → Am is the song’s sad turn. Play the melody with Band only, bending a few notes the second time through.

liner.origins: The melody is a Hasidic nigun (wordless song) from Eastern Europe. Abraham Zvi Idelsohn, a cantor and musicologist in Jerusalem, set Hebrew words to it in 1918 to celebrate the British victory in Palestine; the words (“Let us rejoice”) are often credited to him, though students of the song disagree on how much was his work and how much his student Moshe Nathanson's. The tune's exact earlier history is not settled.
liner.tradition: Danced as a hora, a fast circle dance in which everyone holds hands and the circle speeds up. Klezmer bands play it with clarinet or violin leading, a steady oom-pah pulse underneath, and a faster tempo on each repeat. It is the standard dance at Jewish weddings and bar and bat mitzvahs.
